parts.text:
You read part of an interview. An analyst asked one future user of a software service a series of questions. You decide, for each question, whether it follows up the answer given just before it.

A question follows up the previous answer when it asks about something that answer said: it asks the speaker to explain, give an example of, say more about, or say why of something the answer mentioned, or it picks up a particular thing the answer named. Wording does not matter; a question can follow up an answer without repeating any of its words.

A question does not follow up the previous answer when it turns to something that answer did not mention, even if the speaker said it in an earlier answer, even if it stays with the same broad subject, and even if it is a good question. A general question that could follow any answer, such as whether there is anything else, does not follow up either.

You receive the pairs of the interview after its first question: for each later question, the answer given just before it, and the question.

Reply with JSON only: an object with one key, "questions", a list with exactly one entry for every pair, in the same order. Each entry has "id", the question's id, and "follow_up", true or false.

Q2
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: That's fine, let's take it smaller. What was the very first thing you did when you got to work yesterday?

Q3
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: No problem. Think of any one task you remember doing recently at work. What was it?

Q4
The answer just before it: I keep drones and charging equipment in working order, which includes adding new drones to the fleet, retiring old ones, and setting up charging pads at our sites. I also take drones out of service for repairs and put them back, and send drones to charge. Regulators can ask our company to show how our drones have been looked after.
The question: When you last took a drone out of service for a repair, what happened, step by step?

Q5

The question: How do you usually find out that a drone needs a repair?

Q6
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: You mentioned regulators can ask your company to show how drones have been looked after. What do you have to be able to show them?

Q7
The answer just before it: Regulators can ask our company to show how our drones have been looked after. I don't know any more about what we must show them.
The question: Thinking back over the last few months, which day at work was the worst for you, and what happened?

Q8
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: Is there anything in your work that you double-check yourself, by hand, because you don't fully trust what you're told or shown?

Q9
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: If a new service came in to support your work, what would worry you most about it?

Q10
The answer just before it: I don't know what worries me about a new service.
The question: When something has gone wrong with a drone or a charging pad, what do you need to know first?

Q11
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: Who gives you work, and who do you pass work on to?

Q12
The answer just before it: I don't know who gives me work or who I pass work on to.
The question: You said you add new drones to the fleet. What does adding a drone involve for you?

Q13
The answer just before it: I add new drones to the fleet and set up charging pads at our sites. A company may run a few hundred drones of several models from different manufacturers, which differ in payload, battery range, sensors, and charging connectors. Our company has its own charging pads at its own sites, a few dozen of them.
The question: You also mentioned sending drones to charge. How do you decide which drone goes to which charging pad?

Q14
The answer just before it: I don't know how I decide which drone goes to which charging pad. Our company has a few dozen charging pads at our own sites, and several connector types are in use that are not interchangeable.
The question: What happens when you put a drone back into service after a repair?

Q15
The answer just before it: I take drones out of service for repairs and put them back. I don't know what happens when I put a drone back into service after a repair.
The question: And when a drone is retired, what does that involve?

Q16
The answer just before it: I retire old drones from the fleet. I don't know what else is involved in retiring a drone.
The question: What does setting up a charging pad at one of your sites involve?

Q17
The answer just before it: I set up charging pads at our company's sites. We have our own charging pads at our own sites, a few dozen of them. Several connector types are in use and they are not interchangeable, and pads are never lent to another company.
The question: You said the drone models differ in payload, battery range, sensors, and connectors. Where do those differences cause you trouble in your work?

Q18
The answer just before it: I don't know where those differences cause trouble in my work.
The question: You said pads are never lent to another company. What else about your fleet or sites must stay inside your company?

Q19
The answer just before it: Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. Our company's drones and charging equipment are kept in working order by technicians like me, and we have our own charging pads at our own sites.
The question: When you take a drone out of service, who else is affected by that?

Q20
The answer just before it: I don't know who else is affected when I take a drone out of service.
The question: How do you keep track today of what has been done to each drone?

Q21
The answer just before it: I don't know how I keep track of what has been done to each drone. Repairs and servicing are carried out by technicians, and regulators can ask our company to show how our drones have been looked after.
The question: What can go wrong when a drone is sent to charge?

Q22
The answer just before it: I don't know what can go wrong when a drone is sent to charge.
The question: Is there anything about your work, your drones, or your charging equipment that I haven't asked about and that you think I should know?

Q23
The answer just before it: I keep drones and charging equipment in working order, adding new drones, retiring old ones, and setting up charging pads at our sites. I also take drones out of service for repairs, put them back, and send drones to charge. Regulators can ask our company to show how our drones have been looked after.
The question: From your side, what makes a drone fit to go out on a job?
